source.title: CBSE Senior School Certificate Examination 2025, Physics (042), Q.P. Code 55/4/1
source.subject: physics
source.notes: Paper prints: Series X4YZW, 'SET ~ 1' (text layer; stored as SET-1), Q.P. Code 55/4/1, Maximum Marks 70, Time allowed 3 hours, 33 questions in 5 sections (A: Q1-16 MCQ 1 mark; B: Q17-21 VSA 2 marks; C: Q22-28 SA 3 marks; D: Q29-30 Case Study 4 marks; E: Q31-33 LA 5 marks). No overall choice; internal choice provided in some questions in all sections except A. Session is not printed on the paper. The paper is bilingual: within the QP.zip archive, Q.P. Codes 55/1/1, 55/1/2, 55/1/3, 55/2/1, 55/2/2 and 55/2/3 (checked in that Q.P.-code order, the order they appear in the official zip) all extract to an EMPTY text layer with pdftotext (scanned/image-only pages; 0 non-whitespace characters across all pages) and were SKIPPED per instructions. Q.P. Code 55/4/1 is the first code in the archive with a usable text layer and was used for this pack. Within 55/4/1's own PDF, English and Hindi text alternate by page (Hindi on odd pages, English on even pages, except the cover/instructions on pages 1-2 which are Hindi and page 3 which is the English general instructions); the 'page' field on each question below is the PDF page (1-based) carrying that question's English text. A recurring extraction problem specific to this PDF (beyond the usual dropped Greek letters/degree/ohm signs seen in other CBSE packs) is that a number of MCQ options and even some question-stem clauses are rendered as embedded vector/image glyphs with NO text at all (not even digits) - this affects option (B)-(D) of Q6, and large parts of the Section D case-study MCQ options (Q29 sub-parts (i)-(iii) and (iv)(a); Q30 sub-parts (i)-(ii) and (iv)(a)); in several other places a clause or short phrase is missing outright (e.g. the opening sentence of Q21, the question stem of Q24, part of the Q29 case-study introduction, a physical-quantity word in Q30(iv)(a), the refractive index value in Q33(a)(ii)). Each such loss is flagged per-question in extractionIssues; nothing was invented to fill these gaps. The official marking scheme (XII_042_Physics_MS_55_4_1,2,3.pdf, matching Q.P. Code 55/4/1 in its first ~20-page section, inside 'Physics/042 Physics English Medium/' of the marking-scheme archive) DOES have a usable text layer and was used to source officialAnswer for every question/part; its own text also has some symbol/formula losses (flagged per question where they affect the officialAnswer).

questions.text:
In the given figure, three identical bulbs P, Q and S are connected to a battery.
(i) Compare the brightness of bulbs P and Q with that of bulb S when key K is closed.
(ii) Compare the brightness of the bulbs S and Q when the key K is opened.
Justify your answer in both cases.

officialAnswer.text: (i) Brightness of bulb 'S' will be more than bulbs 'P' and 'Q'; the current through 'S' is twice the current through 'P' and 'Q'. (ii) Brightness of 'S' and 'Q' will be the same; the current through both bulbs is the same. [Alternatively, argued via potential difference: p.d. across 'S' is twice that across 'P'/'Q'; p.d. across 'S' and 'Q' is the same.]

figures.alt: Circuit diagram: bulbs P, Q and S, a key K, and a cell with + and − terminals

questions.text: Find the angle of diffraction (in degrees) for first secondary maximum of the pattern due to diffraction at a single slit. The width of the slit and wavelength of light used are 0·55 mm and 550 nm, respectively.

officialAnswer.text: θ = (2n+1)λ/2a; for the first secondary maximum n = 1, θ = 3λ/2a = (3 × 550×10⁻⁹)/(2 × 0.55×10⁻³); θ = 1.5×10⁻³ radian ≈ 0.086°.

questions.text: An equiconvex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1·55. If the focal length of the lens is 15·0 cm, calculate the radius of curvature of its surfaces.

officialAnswer.text: 1/f = (n₂₁ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂); for an equiconvex lens R₁ = R and R₂ = −R; 1/15 = (1.55 − 1)(2/R); R = 16.5 cm.

questions.text: Calculate the mass of an alpha-particle in atomic mass unit (u). Given, mass of a normal helium atom = 4·002603 u; mass of carbon atom = 1·9926 × 10⁻²⁶ kg.
extractionIssues: Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout (negative power of ten '10 26' → '10⁻²⁶'); check against the PDF

officialAnswer.text: 1 u = (1/12) × mass of carbon atom = 1.9926×10⁻²⁶/12 kg ≈ 1.661×10⁻²⁷ kg; mass of two electrons = 2 × 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg = 0.00109638 u; mass of α-particle = mass of normal helium atom − mass of two electrons = 4.0026030 − 0.00109638 = 4.00150662 u.

questions.text:
In an intrinsic semiconductor, carrier's concentration is 5 × 10⁸ m⁻³. On doping with impurity atoms, the hole concentration becomes 8 × 10¹² m⁻³.
(a) Identify (i) the type of dopant and (ii) the extrinsic semiconductor so formed.
(b) Calculate the electron concentration in the extrinsic semiconductor.

officialAnswer.text: (a)(i) Trivalent dopant. (ii) p-type semiconductor. (b) Electron concentration nₑ = nᵢ²/nₕ = (5×10⁸)²/(8×10¹²); nₑ = 3.125×10⁴ m⁻³.

questions.text:
(i) Derive an expression for the resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of free electrons and relaxation time.
(ii) The figure shows the plot of current through a cross-section of wire over two different time intervals. Compare the charges (Q1 and Q2) that pass through the cross-section during these time intervals.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Total charge transported along E is
IΔt = (e²A/m) τ nΔtE
I/A = (ne²/m) τE
J = (1/ρ) E
ρ = m/(ne²τ)
Alternatively-
Current in the conductor-
I = neAv_d
I/A = ne (eE/m) τ
J = (ne²τ/m) E
J = (1/ρ) E
ρ = m/(ne²τ)
(ii) From given graph
Q₁/Q₂ = A₁ (Area of rectangle)/A₂ (Area of triangle)
Q₁/Q₂ = 2/(3/2)
Q₁ > Q₂

questions.text:
(i) A battery of emf E and internal resistance r is connected to a variable external resistance R.
(I) Obtain the expression for current I in the circuit and the value of maximum current the battery can supply.
(II) Obtain the terminal voltage V across the battery and its maximum possible value.
(ii) The above battery sends a current I1 when R = R1 and a current I2 when R = R2. Obtain the internal resistance of the battery in terms of I1, I2, R1 and R2.

officialAnswer.text: (i)(I) I = E/(R+r); for maximum current, R = 0, so I_max = E/r. (II) V = E − Ir; V_max = E, when I = 0. (ii) I₁R₁ + I₁r = I₂R₂ + I₂r, so r = (I₂R₂ − I₁R₁)/(I₁ − I₂).

questions.text:
(a) Write vector form of Biot-Savart law.
(b) Two insulated long straight wires, each carrying 2·0 A current are kept along xx' and yy' axis as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and direction of resultant magnetic field at point P (4m, 5m).

officialAnswer.text: (a) d𝐁 = (μ₀ I (d𝐥 × r̂))/(4π r²). (b) B₁ (due to wire along xx', at perpendicular distance 5) = μ₀·2·2×10⁻⁷/5 = 8×10⁻⁸ T; B₂ (due to wire along yy', at perpendicular distance 4) = μ₀·2·2×10⁻⁷/4 = 10×10⁻⁸ T; Bnet = B₂ − B₁ = 2×10⁻⁸ T, directed along the −Z axis.

figures.alt: Axes x'x, y'y and z (dashed) with two thick wires along the x and y axes, each with a current arrow I, and a point P at (4, 5)

questions.text:
Two coils '1' and '2' are placed close to each other as shown in the figure. Find the direction of induced current in coil '1' in each of the following situations, justifying your answers :
(a) Coil '2' is moving towards coil '1'.
(b) Coil '2' is moving away from coil '1'.
(c) The resistance connected with coil '2' is increased keeping both the coils stationary.

officialAnswer.text: (a) Coil 2 moving towards Coil 1: induced current in Coil 1 is clockwise (the approaching face of Coil 2 behaves like a south pole, so Coil 1's near face becomes a south pole too, opposing it). (b) Coil 2 moving away: induced current in Coil 1 is anticlockwise. (c) Resistance in Coil 2 increased, both coils stationary: induced current in Coil 1 is anticlockwise while the flux is decreasing, then zero once steady.

figures.alt: Two coils side by side: Coil 2 connected through a variable resistor R2 and a cell between ends M and N; Coil 1 connected to a resistor R1 between ends O and P

questions.text:
(a) State any three characteristics of electromagnetic waves.
(b) Briefly explain how and where the displacement current exists during the charging of a capacitor.

officialAnswer.text: (a) Any three: EM waves carry energy; carry momentum; travel at the speed of light in vacuum; E, B and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular; they are transverse in nature; they need no medium to propagate; they consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields. (b) During charging of a capacitor, the time-varying electric field/flux between the plates induces the displacement current, which exists in the region between the plates of the capacitor.

questions.text:
A double slit set-up was initially placed in a tank filled with water and the interference pattern was obtained using a laser light. When water is replaced by a transparent liquid of refractive index n > n(water), what will be the effect on the following ?
(a) Speed, frequency and wavelength of the light of laser beam.
(b) The fringe width, shape of interference fringes and shift in the position of central maximum.
extractionIssues: Subscript flattened: 'nwater' (refractive index of water, printed as a subscript) reproduced as 'n(water)'; see page 17

officialAnswer.text: (a) Speed of light decreases; frequency remains unaffected; wavelength decreases. (b) Fringe width decreases; shape of the fringes does not change; position of the central maximum does not change.

questions.text:
Explain the following observations using Einstein's photoelectric equation :
(a) Photoelectric emission does not occur from a surface when the frequency of the light incident on it is less than a certain minimum value.
(b) It is the frequency, and not the intensity of the incident light which affects the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
(c) The cut-off voltage (V₀) versus frequency (ν) of the incident light curve is a straight line with a slope h/e.

officialAnswer.text: (a) Einstein's equation: hν = hν₀ + K_max ⇒ K_max = h(ν − ν₀); for ν < ν₀, K_max would be negative, so photoelectric emission is not possible. (b) K_max = h(ν − ν₀) ⇒ K_max depends only on frequency, not on intensity. (c) eV₀ = hν − hν₀ ⇒ V₀ = (h/e)ν − (h/e)ν₀, the equation of a straight line (y = mx + c) with slope h/e.

questions.text:
(a) What are majority and minority charge carriers of p-type and n-type semiconductors ?
(b) Explain briefly the formation of diffusion current and drift current in a p-n junction diode.

officialAnswer.text: (a) p-type: majority carriers – holes, minority carriers – electrons. n-type: majority carriers – electrons, minority carriers – holes. (b) Diffusion current: due to the concentration gradient across the junction, holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side. Drift current: due to the electric field at the junction, electrons on the p-side move to the n-side and holes on the n-side move to the p-side.

questions.text:
A parallel plate capacitor consists of two conducting plates kept generally parallel to each other at a distance. When the capacitor is charged, the charge resides on the inner surfaces of the plates and an electric field is set up between them. Thus, electrostatic energy is stored in the capacitor.
The figure shows three large square metallic plates, each of side 'L' held parallel and equidistant from each other. The space between P₁ and P₂ and P₂ and P₃ is completely filled with mica sheets of dielectric constant 'K'. The plate P₂ is connected to point A and other plates P₁ and P₃ are connected to point B. Point A is maintained at a positive potential with respect to point B and the potential difference between A and B is V.

(i) The capacitance of the system between A and B will be :
(A) ε₀KL²/d
(B) ε₀KL²/(2d)
(C) 2ε₀KL²/d
(D) 2ε₀Kd/L²

(ii) The charge on plate P₁ is :
(A) ε₀VKL²/(2d)
(B) ε₀VKL²/d
(C) 2ε₀VKL²/d
(D) ε₀VKL²/(4d)

(iii) The electric field in the region between P₁ and P₂ is :
(A) V/d
(B) 2V/d
(C) V/(2d)
(D) d/V

(iv) (a) The separation between the plates of same area (L²) of a parallel plate air capacitor having capacitance equal to that of this system, will be :
(A) d/K
(B) 2d/K
(C) d/(2K)
(D) d/(4K)
OR
(b) If the source of potential difference applied between A and B is removed, and then A and B are connected by a conducting wire, the net charge on the system will be :
(A) ε₀VKL²/(4d)
(B) ε₀VKL²/(2d)
(C) ε₀VKL²/d
(D) Zero
extractionIssues: Internal choice ('OR') in sub-part (iv) is kept inline within this case-based question's text, not split into a separate entry, as it applies to only one of the four sub-parts

officialAnswer.text:
(i) (C) C = 2ε₀KL²/d
(ii) (B) Charge on P1 = ε₀VKL²/d
(iii) (A) E = V/d
(iv)(a) (C) d/2K
OR
(iv)(b) (D) Zero

questions.text:
A hydrogen atom consists of an electron revolving in a circular orbit of radius r with certain velocity v around a proton located at the nucleus of the atom. The electrostatic force of attraction between the revolving electron and the proton provides the requisite centripetal force to keep it in the orbit. According to Bohr's model, an electron can revolve only in certain stable orbits. The angular momentum of the electron in these orbits is some integral multiple of h/2π, where h is the Planck's constant.
Further, when an electron makes a transition from one orbit of higher energy to that of lower energy, a photon is emitted having energy equal to the difference between energies of the initial and final states. Assuming the mass and charge of an electron as m and e respectively, answer the following questions.

(i) The expression for the speed of electron v in terms of radius of the orbit (r) and physical constant (K = 1/(4πε₀)) is :
(A) Ke²/(mr)
(B) Ke²/(mr²)
(C) √(Ke²/(mr))
(D) √(Ke²/(mr²))

(ii) The total energy of the atom in terms of r and physical constant K is :
(A) Ke²/r
(B) −Ke²/(2r)
(C) Ke²/(2r)
(D) (3/2)(Ke²/r)

(iii) A photon of wavelength 500 nm is emitted when an electron makes a transition from one state to the other state in an atom. The change in the total energy of the electron and change in its kinetic energy in eV as per Bohr's model, respectively will be :
(A) 2·48, −2·48
(B) −1·24, 1·24
(C) −2·48, 2·48
(D) 1·24, −1·24

(iv) (a) In Bohr's model of hydrogen atom, the frequency of revolution of electron in its nth orbit is proportional to :
(A) n
(B) 1/n
(C) 1/n²
(D) 1/n³
OR
(b) An electron makes a transition from −3·4 eV state to the ground state in hydrogen atom. Its radius of orbit changes by : (radius of orbit of electron in ground state = 0·53 Å)
(A) 0·53 Å
(B) 1·06 Å
(C) 1·59 Å
(D) 2·12 Å
extractionIssues: Internal choice ('OR') in sub-part (iv) is kept inline within this case-based question's text, not split into a separate entry, as it applies to only one of the four sub-parts

questions.text:
(i) Two point charges +q and –q are held at (a, 0) and (–a, 0) in x-y plane. Obtain an expression for the net electric field due to the charges at a point (0, y). Hence, find electric field at a far off point (y >> a).
(ii) Three point charges of –2 nC, –1 nC, and +5 nC are kept at the vertices A, B and C of an equilateral triangle of side 0·2 m. Find the total amount of work done in shifting the charges from A to A1, B to B1 and C to C1. Here A1, B1 and C1 are the midpoints of sides AB, BC and CA, respectively.

officialAnswer.text: (i) E = −(2qa)/(4πε₀(y²+a²)^(3/2)) p̂, directed opposite to the dipole moment; at a far-off point (y >> a), E ≈ −(2qa)/(4πε₀y³) p̂. (ii) U₁ = (1/4πε₀)[qAqB/AB + qCqA/AC + qCqB/BC] = −5.85×10⁻⁷ J; U₂ (with A1, B1, C1 as midpoints) = −11.7×10⁻⁷ J; W = U₂ − U₁ = −5.85×10⁻⁷ J.

questions.text:
(i) Show that Gauss's theorem is consistent with Coulomb's law. Using it, derive an expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius r at a point at a distance y from the centre of the shell such that (I) y > r, and (II) y < r.
(ii) A point charge of +2 nC is kept at the origin of a three-dimensional coordinate system. Find the type and magnitude of the charge which should be kept at (0, 0, −6m) so that the potential due to the system becomes zero at (0, 0, 2m).

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Gauss's theorem is based on the inverse square dependence on distance contained in the coulomb's law.
Alternatively-
According to Gauss's theorem
∮E⃗.ds⃗ = q/ε₀
E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²)
According to Coulomb's law, force on charge q₀ in this field
F = (1/4πε₀)(qq₀/r²)
Therefore, Gauss's law is consistent with Coulomb's law
(I) For y > r
Electric flux through Gaussian surface E×4πy²
The charge enclosed by the surface σ×4πr²
Using Gauss theorem
E(4πy²) = σ4πr²/ε₀
E⃗ = (q/(4πε₀y²)) r̂
(II) For y < r
The charge enclosed by Gaussian surface = 0
Using Gauss theorem
Electric flux = E(4πy²) = 0
i.e. E = 0 (y < r)
(ii) Let the charge is kept at A be q
Potential at point B due to charge at the origin O and charge (q) at A
V = V₁ + V₂
V = (1/4πε₀)[2×10⁻⁹/2 + q/(6+2)]
(1/4πε₀)[10⁻⁹ + q/8] = 0
q = −8×10⁻⁹ C

questions.text:
(i) State Lenz's law and explain how this law is a consequence of conservation of energy principle.
(ii) A square shaped loop of side l/2 is initially lying outside a region of uniform magnetic field B⃗ as shown in the figure. The loop is moved towards right with a constant velocity v⃗ till it goes out of the region of magnetic field.
(I) What will be the directions of induced current when the loop enters the field and when it leaves the field ?
(II) Draw the plots showing the variation of magnetic flux ϕ linked with the loop with time t and variation of induced emf E with time t. Mark the relevant values of E, ϕ and t on the graphs.

officialAnswer.text: (i) Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it; this is consistent with conservation of energy since mechanical work done to move the magnet/loop converts into electrical energy. (ii)(I) Induced current is anticlockwise while the loop enters the field and clockwise while it leaves. (II) [Graphs of flux vs t and emf vs t with marked values — not reproducible as text.]

questions.text:
(i) Differentiate between peak and rms values of alternating current. How are they related ?
(ii) A current element X is connected across an ac source of emf V = V₀ sin 2πνt. It is found that the voltage leads the current in phase by π/2 radian. If element X was replaced by element Y, the voltage lags behind the current in phase by π/2 radian.
(I) Identify elements X and Y by drawing phasor diagrams.
(II) Obtain the condition of resonance when both elements X and Y are connected in series to the source and obtain expression for resonant frequency. What is the impedance value in this case ?

officialAnswer.text: (i) Peak value is the maximum value of the alternating current; rms value is the equivalent dc current that would produce the same average power/heating effect. Relation: I_rms = I₀/√2. (ii)(I) X = Inductor (L), Y = Capacitor (C). (II) Impedance Z = XL − XC; at resonance Z = 0, so XL = XC ⇒ ω = 1/√(LC), i.e. ν = 1/(2π√(LC)); impedance at resonance Z = 0.

questions.text:
(i) An object is placed 30 cm from a thin convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The lens forms a sharp image on a screen. If a thin concave lens is placed in contact with the convex lens, the sharp image on the screen is formed when the screen is moved by 45 cm from its initial position. Calculate the focal length of the concave lens.
(ii) Calculate the angle of minimum deviation of an equilateral prism. The refractive index of the prism is √3. Calculate the angle of incidence for this case of minimum deviation also.

officialAnswer.text: (i) For the convex lens alone: 1/f₁ = 1/v₁ − 1/u₁ ⇒ 1/10 = 1/v₁ − 1/(−30) ⇒ v₁ = 15 cm. For the combination (screen moved by 45 cm, so v₃ = 15+45 = 60 cm): 1/f₃ = 1/60 − 1/(−30) ⇒ f₃ = 20 cm. For the concave lens: 1/f₃ = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ ⇒ 1/f₂ = 1/20 − 1/10 ⇒ f₂ = −20 cm. (ii) μ = sin((A+δm)/2)/sin(A/2); with A = 60° and μ = √3, δm = 60° and the angle of incidence i = (A+δm)/2 = 60°.

questions.text:
(i) A physics teacher wants to demonstrate interference with the help of double slit experiment using a laser beam of 633 nm wavelength. Since the hall is large enough, interference pattern is formed on the wall 5·0 m from the slits. For clear and comfortable view by all the students they want the fringe width 5 mm.
(I) Find the slit separation for obtaining the desired interference pattern.
(II) How far will the first minimum be from the central maximum ?
(ii) A parallel beam of light of wavelength 650 nm passes through a slit of width 0·6 mm. The diffraction pattern is obtained on a screen kept 60 cm away from the slit. Find the distance between first order minima on both sides of the central maximum.

officialAnswer.text: (i)(I) d = Dλ/β = (5 × 633×10⁻⁹)/(5×10⁻³) = 633×10⁻⁶ m = 633 μm. (II) First minimum from central maximum, x = (2n−1)λD/2d with n=1: x = (633×10⁻⁹ × 5)/(2×5×10⁻³) = 316.5×10⁻⁶ m = 316.5 μm. (ii) Distance between first-order minima on both sides, W = 2Dλ/d = (2×650×10⁻⁹×60×10⁻²)/(0.6×10⁻³) = 1.3×10⁻³ m.
